text: Once an enterprise accepts it's running hybrid, the first practical problem is mundane but non-negotiable: how does a server in an on-premises data center actually talk to a VM in an Azure VNet or an AWS VPC? This lesson covers the real connectivity and identity patterns that join on-prem back to the cloud, so the two behave like one estate instead of two networks that merely happen to reach each other over the internet.

There are three real options. A site-to-site VPN is an encrypted IPsec tunnel over the public internet — fast to stand up, genuinely inexpensive, and entirely sufficient for a lot of workloads, though throughput and latency aren't guaranteed. Azure ExpressRoute and AWS Direct Connect are dedicated private circuits that skip the public internet entirely, giving you predictable bandwidth and latency at real cost and real provisioning lead time. Enterprises frequently run both together — the dedicated circuit as the primary path, with a VPN configured as automatic failover if it goes down.

Concretely, an ExpressRoute circuit terminates at a connectivity provider's edge and peers with your hub VNet through an ExpressRoute gateway at a set bandwidth, using private peering. A Direct Connect connection works the same way on the AWS side — a physical connection from a colocation facility, a private virtual interface, peering with a transit gateway or hub VPC. Neither one ever touches the public internet, which is the entire reason they exist.

A connected network only solves reachability — it doesn't solve who's allowed to log in. The realistic hybrid identity pattern is extending your existing Active Directory, never duplicating it. Microsoft Entra Connect syncs or federates on-prem AD into Microsoft Entra ID. On AWS, AD Connector proxies authentication back to your existing on-prem AD, while Managed Microsoft AD runs an actual AD domain in AWS that trusts your on-prem forest. And once you have multiple sites and multiple cloud networks, hub-and-spoke keeps it manageable: on-prem connectivity terminates once, in the hub, and every other network inherits it through that single relationship.

That's the connectivity and identity layer sorted — but connectivity alone doesn't give you one control plane for actually managing that infrastructure day to day. Next lesson covers the two real technologies built for exactly that: Azure Arc, which brings on-premises and multi-cloud servers and Kubernetes clusters under Azure's control plane, and AWS Outposts, which puts actual AWS infrastructure physically on-premises.
